docs.title: Welcome to MMKS Knowledge Base
docs.text:
MMKS is a centralized knowledge platform designed for Mammotion's distributors, dealers, and authorized service partners.

It provides structured product information, operational guidelines, technical knowledge, and troubleshooting resources to support partners throughout the product lifecycle — from product selection and customer guidance to installation, diagnostics, and technical service.

The knowledge base supports different partner roles and competency levels (L1–L4), enabling users to access relevant information according to their responsibilities and technical expertise.

docs.title: 🎓 Learning Path | L1–L4
docs.text:
MMKS supports a progressive competency framework for external partners, from basic product knowledge to advanced technical service capabilities.

Level Knowledge Focus L1 – Product & Sales Product understanding, model selection, basic App operation, and customer guidance L2 – Installation & Support Product setup, installation procedures, operational guidance, and initial issue identification L3 – Technical Troubleshooting System-level understanding, structured diagnostics, and technical issue resolution L4 – Advanced Technical Service Advanced diagnostics, component-level analysis, repair procedures, and complex issue handling

Learning Guidance

Knowledge resources may be relevant to multiple competency levels. Users are encouraged to explore topics based on their responsibilities, technical expertise, and service needs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This section provides structured troubleshooting resources for Mammotion's distributors, dealers, and authorized service partners.

It covers common product issues, symptom identification, diagnostic procedures, possible causes, and recommended solutions across software, hardware, positioning, navigation, connectivity, and other operational systems.

The goal is to help partners identify issues efficiently, perform appropriate troubleshooting steps, resolve common problems, and determine when further technical support or escalation is required.

docs.title: ⚡ Power, Hardware & Software
docs.text:
• Battery & Charging Diagnose charging failures, battery-related issues, power supply problems, and abnormal charging behavior.

  • Firmware & App Troubleshoot firmware updates, App connectivity, software errors, and unexpected system behavior.

  • Hardware Identify hardware-related faults, component malfunctions, and physical damage.

docs.title: 🗺️ Mapping, Positioning & Navigation
docs.text:
• Mapping Troubleshoot map creation, boundary editing, map storage, and mapping-related errors.

  • Navigation & Motion Control Diagnose movement abnormalities, path planning issues, wheel behavior, and motion control failures.

  • Obstacle Avoidance Investigate obstacle detection problems, abnormal avoidance behavior, and related sensor issues.

  • Positioning Identify localization failures, positioning instability, RTK/GNSS-related issues, and other positioning abnormalities.

docs.title: 📡 Connectivity & Other Issues
docs.text:
• WiFi & Bluetooth & 4G Troubleshoot wireless connectivity, network configuration, communication failures, and remote access issues.

  • Quality Issue Review known product quality issues, reported abnormalities, and relevant identification or handling guidance.

docs.title: 🛠️ Recommended Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
Follow a structured approach to identify and resolve product issues.

Step 1 — Identify the Issue

Confirm the reported symptoms, affected functions, error messages, and conditions under which the issue occurs.

Step 2 — Verify Product Information

Check the product model, hardware version, firmware version, App version, and relevant operating conditions.

Step 3 — Perform Initial Checks

Inspect the basic operating conditions, power supply, connectivity, installation environment, and other relevant factors.

Step 4 — Follow Diagnostic Procedures

Select the appropriate troubleshooting category and perform the recommended checks in sequence.

Step 5 — Verify the Solution

Confirm whether the issue has been resolved and whether the robot has returned to normal operation.

Step 6 — Escalate if Necessary

If the issue remains unresolved or requires advanced diagnostics, repair, or component replacement, escalate it through the appropriate technical support channel.

docs.title: 💡 User Tips
docs.text:
Search by Symptom or Error Code

Use the search bar to find troubleshooting information based on error codes, warning messages, product models, or observed symptoms.

Check Basic Conditions First

Before performing advanced diagnostics, verify the power supply, network connection, installation conditions, and current software versions.

Follow the Recommended Sequence

Complete the applicable diagnostic steps in order. Avoid replacing hardware or performing unnecessary operations before identifying the likely cause.

Collect Relevant Information

When escalating an unresolved issue, provide the product model, firmware version, error messages, observed symptoms, troubleshooting steps already performed, and relevant logs or images when available.

Safety & Service Notice

Follow applicable safety instructions before inspection or maintenance. Hardware disassembly, electrical testing, and component replacement should only be performed by appropriately trained and authorized personnel.

Knowledge Scope

This section supports issue identification, remote troubleshooting, and technical problem resolution. Advanced repairs and service operations should follow the relevant authorized service procedures.

docs.title: Auto-Recharge Issue - Vehicle Bumps Station and Exits After Returning, No Charge / Docking Abnormal
docs.text:
Error Code:

  • 1200 Repeatedly entering/leaving dock / bumping dock
  • 2729 Adapter voltage low

Solution:

  1. Check that the charging station is installed on the ground and that the device's contacts are fully in contact with the charging station's contacts.
  2. Check whether the charging contact strips on the rear of the mower and the charging station's probes are dirty or corroded; clean them if necessary.
  3. Check whether the connection port between the charging station's power cable and the adapter is loose; re-plug it if necessary.
  4. Test the voltage of the charging station contacts and the adapter. If abnormal, send a replacement adapter.

Query Page:

  1. Check the Device Profile and Self-check modules to confirm whether the robot's hardware connections are normal.
  2. Based on the corresponding error code, preliminarily determine the type and possible cause of the robot's fault.

If not solved: Needs Repair

docs.text:

  • 1203 Return-to-dock failed
  • 1214 Path blocked by obstacle

  1. Check for obstacles around the area. Clear any obstacles to ensure the path is wide enough (LUBA 3: minimum path width is 70cm).
  2. If there are no obstacles or clearing them does not help, check whether the LiDAR / vision module is dirty. Clean it and keep it regularly cleaned.
  3. If there is no dirt or cleaning does not help, check whether there is a virtual wall / no-go zone blocking the path in the app map.
  4. If there is no virtual wall or re-trying does not help, check whether a connecting path is missing between the target zone and other zones. If so, create the path.

After slow-flashing for a few minutes, the device will power off and the indicator will go off if the RTK is not powered or the device is not exposed to sunlight.

  3. Verify and ensure that the adapter bracket nut is tight. Remove the cutter disk and check whether the noise still exists.
  4. If there is no noise after removing the cutter disk, check whether the cutter disk is worn and whether any screws are loose.
  5. If the noise still exists after replacing the cutter disk / screws, and the noise comes from the wheel hub motor, listen carefully to identify which wheel. With the machine powered off, check the wheel's exterior for damage and manually rotate the wheel to see whether it rotates smoothly. If not, clear any grass tangled in the wheel hub and try again. docs.title: Algorithm Principle Knowledge
docs.text: The robot algorithm system is responsible for converting the information acquired by sensors into motion decisions that the robot can execute, enabling the robot to autonomously complete positioning, environment understanding, path planning, obstacle avoidance, and automatic recharging. A typical autonomous movement process can be understood as follows: the robot first determines its own status through information such as GNSS/RTK, IMU, Camera, and wheel speed, and obtains its own position and environment map via Localization and SLAM; Navigation calculates the travel route based on the current position, target position and the map;Obstacle Avoidance dynamically adjusts the route based on real-time environmental information; when the task is completed or the battery level is low, the Docking system is responsible for guiding the robot to return and accurately dock at the charging station. Therefore, the algorithm modules can be divided into Localization, Mapping \& SLAM, Navigation \& Obstacle Avoidance, and Docking four main sections.

docs.title: Static Planning and Control
docs.text:
• Advantages: Fixed boundaries, relatively simple logic, and high consistency; the map viewed by users is consistent with the map used by the robot.

  • Disadvantages: It has poor adaptability to positioning errors, positioning drift, and changes in the actual environment, and is prone to problems related to missing cutting or boundary control in boundaries/narrow passages and complex areas.

docs.title: Dynamic Planning and Control
docs.text:
• Advantages: It is mainly reflected in the dynamic map logic. To adapt to the positioning error of about 10 centimeters in vision, the boundary will be dynamically corrected during the operation, and reset to the user's initial map after the operation is completed, so as to avoid user misjudgment. It can improve the boundary coverage rate, operation continuity and adaptability in complex scenarios.

  • Disadvantages: The planning and control logic is more complex, and the actual running trajectory may have a slight deviation from the user's initial map

docs.title: 1.1 Basic Principles of Positioning
docs.text:
The core task of Localization is to continuously estimate the robot's Pose, which refers to "where the robot is" and "which direction it is facing". For ground mobile robots, this can be simply understood as X, Y Position + Heading. A robot does not "know" its own position directly; instead, it continuously calculates and updates its position state based on information provided by multiple sensors.

Positioning information can be mainly divided into Absolute Position and Relative Motion. GNSS/RTK can provide the position of the robot relative to the global or working area coordinate system, so it belongs to absolute positioning information; while IMU, Wheel Odometry and visual motion information mainly tell the robot "how much it has moved from the previous position", which belongs to relative motion information.Actual robots usually use two types of information simultaneously: absolute positioning is responsible for the long-term position reference, while relative positioning is in charge of short-term continuous motion estimation.

docs.title: 1.2 GNSS and RTK
docs.text: GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) calculates the position of a robot by receiving signals transmitted by multiple satellites. A robot needs to simultaneously acquire information from multiple satellites and estimate its own position based on the satellites' positions and signal transmission data. GPS, Galileo, BeiDou and GLONASS all fall under the category of GNSS systems.Conventional GNSS typically only provides meter-level positioning accuracy, so for robots that need to perform high-precision operations along virtual boundaries or planned paths, relying solely on ordinary GNSS is usually insufficient. To further improve positioning accuracy, RTK Correction Data can be introduced on the basis of GNSS.

docs.title: 1.2.1 RTK — Local Reference Station
docs.text:
The core principle of RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) is to utilize a Reference Station with a known accurate position as a position reference. Both the reference station and the robot receive GNSS satellite signals simultaneously; since the reference station’s own position is known, it can calculate positioning errors based on the received satellite information and generate Correction Data. After receiving these correction data, the robot combines them with the satellite information it receives, thereby obtaining a more precise position result.

The basic principle can be understood as follows:

GNSS Satellite Signal + Local Reference Station Correction → High-Precision Robot Position

In this approach, an RTK Reference Station usually needs to be installed near the robot's working area. The Reference Station itself requires good sky visibility to stably receive satellite signals, and a communication link for Correction Data from the Reference Station to the robot also needs to be established. Therefore, traditional RTK positioning relies simultaneously on the satellite signal at the robot end, the satellite signal at the base station end, and the correction data communication between the base station and the robot.

When installing an RTK base station, the top priority is "co-view", which ensures that the rover and the base lock onto the same satellite.

For example: 1. It is best to avoid having walls between the base station and the robots; 2. It is advisable not to install the base station in overly tall flower clusters. These measures can better ensure the elevation angle of the base station's coverage.

Network RTK (VRS, Virtual RTK Station): A virtual reference station near the user is generated via cloud-based multi-station networking. It requires the device to have a stable 4G network, and a network disconnection within 1 minute will not affect positioning accuracy.

docs.title: 1.2.2 NetRTK — Network RTK
docs.text:
The basic positioning principle adopted by NetRTK (Network RTK) still falls into the category of RTK, but it differs in the source of Correction Data. Instead of requiring users to set up a local Reference Station in their garden, it utilizes the already deployed GNSS Reference Station Network to deliver RTK Correction Data to robots via network services.

The basic principle can be understood as follows:

GNSS Satellite Signal + Network RTK Correction → High-Precision Robot Position

The robot first acquires satellite information via GNSS, and meanwhile obtains the Correction Data provided by the NetRTK service through network connections such as 4G / Wi-Fi / Internet, then combines the two sets of information to calculate a high-precision position.

Therefore, the core difference between RTK and NetRTK is not that "one uses satellites while the other uses networks". Both require the robot to directly receive GNSS satellite signals, and the difference mainly lies in the source and transmission mode of RTK Correction Data. The Correction Data of Local RTK mainly comes from nearby local Reference Stations, while the Correction Data of NetRTK is sourced from a remote Reference Station Network and transmitted to the robot via the Internet.

It can be simply understood as:

Local RTK: Satellite → Robot + Local Reference Station → Correction → Robot

NetRTK: Satellite → Robot + Reference Station Network → Internet → Correction → Robot

One of the advantages of NetRTK is that it reduces the need for users to install and maintain local RTK Reference Stations on their own, but it also increases reliance on network connectivity and NetRTK Service Availability.Therefore, when NetRTK fails to work properly, in addition to checking GNSS Satellite Reception, it is also necessary to consider whether the robot can connect to the Internet normally, whether Correction Data can be obtained normally, and whether the relevant services are available.

docs.title: 1.2.3 RTK Position Status
docs.text:
Whether the Correction Data comes from Local RTK or NetRTK, the robot ultimately needs to calculate its own position based on GNSS information and the Correction Data. RTK positioning typically has different states, such as Single / Float / Fixed.

Single means that the robot mainly relies on ordinary GNSS information for positioning, and a valid high-precision RTK solution has not usually been obtained at this time. Float means that the system has obtained RTK Correction Data and started high-precision calculation, but there is still certain uncertainty in the positioning result. Fixed means that the system has obtained a stable high-precision RTK solution, which is usually the most ideal state for high-precision path control.

Therefore, "Correction Data connected" does not equate to "RTK has been Fixed". A robot requires both valid Correction Data and sufficiently good GNSS Satellite Reception to obtain a stable high-precision position.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Environmental Influence
docs.text:
Neither Local RTK nor NetRTK can address all GNSS environmental issues. Buildings, high walls, eaves and dense trees may block the satellite signals received by robots; walls, glass, metal structures and other objects may also cause signal reflection, resulting in Multipath effect, which degrades positioning quality.

Therefore, even if the NetRTK network is properly connected or the Local RTK Reference Station is functioning normally, if the robot itself is located in a severely occluded area, there may still be cases where Fixed switches to Float, positioning accuracy degrades, or high-precision position cannot be obtained temporarily.

From the perspective of Dealer Troubleshooting, the RTK positioning conditions can be simply understood as three parts:

GNSS Signal Quality + Correction Data Availability + Communication Quality → RTK Position Quality

For Local RTK, attention shall be paid to Robot GNSS, Reference Station GNSS and Correction Communication simultaneously; for NetRTK, focus shall be placed on Robot GNSS, Internet Connection and Network Correction Service.This can help identify whether the problem stems from the satellite environment, the Correction Data link, or network/communication conditions.

docs.title: 1.3 IMU \& Wheel Odometry
docs.text:
RTK can provide an accurate position reference, but it cannot independently describe the instantaneous motion changes of a robot, so the robot also requires IMU and Wheel Odometry to provide high-frequency motion information.

An IMU typically perceives the linear and rotational motions of a robot via an accelerometer and a gyroscope. For instance, when a robot starts to turn left, the gyroscope can rapidly detect changes in angular velocity; when the robot traverses a slope or tilts, the IMU can also detect changes in its attitude.

Wheel Odometry leverages the Encoder information of motors or wheels to estimate the moving distance of the robot based on the rotation amount of the wheels. For a differential-drive robot, if the travel distances of the left and right wheels are identical, the robot will basically move in a straight line; if the travel distances of the left and right wheels differ, the robot will turn.

However, wheel odometry has a critical limitation: Wheel Rotation ≠ Always Actual Movement. If the robot slips on wet grass, muddy terrain, or a slope, the wheels may have rotated by a certain distance, but the actual distance the robot travels will be shorter. As a result, the error of wheel odometry will gradually accumulate over time.

docs.title: 1.4 Sensor Fusion Multi-sensor Fusion
docs.text:
As different sensors each have their own limitations, robots typically combine multiple information sources through Sensor Fusion. For example, RTK can provide a long-term and accurate position reference, but may be subject to occlusion in a short period; IMU features a fast update rate, but will generate drift after long-term use; Wheel Odometry can stably describe the normal driving process, but is affected by skidding; Camera can use environmental features to assist in judging motion and position, but is influenced by lighting and lens conditions.

Therefore, the system continuously compares the information from different sensors and estimates the most reliable Robot Pose based on the current information quality. Its basic logic can be understood as follows:

GNSS/RTK + IMU + Wheel Odometry + Vision → Sensor Fusion → Robot Pose

This is also why a short-term drop in RTK signal does not necessarily mean that the robot immediately loses its positioning. The system can rely on other sensors to continue estimating motion, but if a reliable absolute position reference is missing for too long, the positioning error will usually gradually increase.

docs.title: Mapping \& SLAM Mapping and Simultaneous Localization
2.1 Basic Principles of Mapping
docs.text:
Localization addresses the question of "Where am I? ", while Mapping addresses that of "What does the environment look like? ". Robots continuously observe their surroundings via cameras, LiDAR or other environmental sensors, and then, based on their own position, place this environmental information into the correct spatial locations to build a map.

The map used internally by the robot is not necessarily identical to the map displayed to the user in the App. Depending on different functions, the system may simultaneously maintain the boundaries of the working area, obstacle information, navigable areas, restricted zones, and the internal map for Navigation.

A common map representation is Grid Map. The system divides the environment into numerous small grids, each of which can be marked as Free, Occupied or Unknown, meaning "traversable", "obstacle-present" or "unconfirmed" respectively. The robot can then determine which areas are passable based on this information.

Navigation also frequently utilizes Cost Map. Instead of simply dividing the space into "traversable" and "untraversable", it assigns different traversal costs to various regions. For instance, the location of an obstacle is impassable, while areas close to obstacles, though passable, carry higher risks and thus incur higher costs. Navigation can leverage this information to select a safer route.

docs.title: 2.2 Basic Principles of SLAM
docs.text:
The full name of SLAM is Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, which refers to simultaneous localization and mapping. It addresses the problem of mutual dependence between localization and mapping: building an accurate map requires knowing the robot's position, while using the environment for localization in turn requires a map as a reference.

The basic working process of SLAM can be simply understood as follows: as the robot moves, the camera or LiDAR continuously observes the surrounding environment; the system compares the environmental changes observed in two consecutive observations, and meanwhile combines motion information such as IMU and wheel odometry to estimate where the robot has moved from its previous position; then it adds the new environmental information to the map and keeps updating the robot's position.

Therefore, it can be simply expressed as follows:

Robot Motion + Sensor Observation → Pose Estimation → Map Update

For example, when a robot sees a tree for the first time, it will record the position of the tree relative to the robot. When the robot continues to move and sees the tree again from another angle, it can further judge its own movement by comparing environmental features and correcting the positional relationship in the map.

docs.title: 2.3 Visual SLAM \& LiDAR SLAM
docs.text:
Depending on the main environmental sensors used, SLAM can take different forms.

Visual SLAM primarily uses cameras to determine a robot's motion by comparing environmental features across consecutive images. For instance, when the position of the same stationary object shifts in successive frames, the system can leverage this change to estimate the motion of both the camera and the robot.

LiDAR SLAM leverages laser ranging to acquire the distance and geometric contour of the surrounding environment, and compares the scan results obtained by the robot at different positions. If identical walls, trees or other structures exist in the two scans, the system can estimate how the robot has moved based on these geometric relationships.

The two solutions have their respective characteristics: Camera can obtain rich visual and semantic information, but it is susceptible to the influence of lighting, stains and changes in environmental appearance; LiDAR can directly acquire distance and geometric information, and is generally insensitive to lighting changes, yet it may also be affected by the environmental structure, occlusion and sensor operating conditions.

There are also different positioning methods when combined with RTK:

docs.title: RTK+Vision/RTK+Lidar
docs.text:
It relies on the VIO visual-inertial odometry, and the error can be as low as only 1%.

VIO: By fusing data from cameras and inertial measurement units (IMUs), it calculates the continuous displacement and attitude changes of a robot over short periods in real time

SLAM: It refers to the technology of constructing a map of the surrounding environment while determining the robot's current position on the map based on sensor data.

Lidar is mainly used for extending the lifespan of the system, and it can generally cover a distance of around 60 meters.

docs.title: Vision+RTK
docs.text:
Visual-only localization: it will lead to the problem that the robot cannot work at night (around sunset), and since visual localization requires a large number of stored memory points, the storable map area will be relatively smaller accordingly.

When paired with RTK, it can expand the working area, support nighttime operations, and reduce memory pressure.

In scenarios where visual positioning fails (such as in forests and open areas), RTK can function as a repositioning solution.

(When a robot is in an open environment, visual localization only provides a single viewing angle, so the robot rotates to supplement the field of view.)

docs.title: Lidar+RTK
docs.text:
If the robot simply relies on LiDAR for positioning, it will easily encounter problems such as getting stuck, being unable to move, and being unable to re-localize.

Due to the forward-tilted installation, the radar does not achieve full 360-degree coverage, which will also trigger a rotation action.

docs.title: 2.4 Drift \& Loop Closure
docs.text:
An important concept in SLAM is Drift. Every time a robot moves, there is a very small error in its position estimation. If the robot continues to operate, these small errors may gradually accumulate, resulting in a deviation between the position the robot perceives and its actual position.

To reduce such cumulative errors, SLAM can leverage Loop Closure. For example, after a robot travels around a garden and returns to a location it has passed by earlier, if the system recognizes that "this is a place we have been to before", it can use this known correspondence to correct the previously accumulated errors in position and map.

Therefore, SLAM does not simply and continuously add new environmental information to the map; instead, it is an ongoing observation → localization → mapping → reconfirmation → correction process.

docs.title: 3.1 Basic Principles of Navigation
docs.text:
When a robot knows its own position and has a map, it needs to decide "how to get from the current position to the target position", and Navigation is responsible for completing this process.

Navigation typically requires several basic inputs: Current Pose, Target Position, Map, and Real-Time Obstacle Information. The system calculates a traversable path based on these inputs, and further converts the path into steering and movement commands that the robot can actually execute.

Therefore, it can be simply understood as follows:

Current Position + Target + Map → Path Planning → Motion Command

For robotic lawn mowers, Navigation is not only used to travel from point A to point B, but also covers the movement from the charging station to the working area, transitions between different Zones, and the return trip once the task is completed.

docs.title: 3.2 Global Planning \& Local Planning
docs.text:
Navigation can generally be divided into two layers: Global Planning and Local Planning.

The Global Planner calculates the general direction from the current position to the target position based on the overall map. For example, when a robot needs to move from the front yard to the backyard, the Global Planner will determine the overall route according to boundaries, restricted areas and known obstacles.

The Local Planner is responsible for the actual movement of the robot in its current vicinity. Even if the Global Path has been determined, people, pets or temporary objects may still suddenly appear in the real environment, so the robot needs to continuously adjust its short-distance movement according to real-time perception results.

It can be simply understood as:

Global Planner: What's the overall direction we should take?

Local Planner: How exactly to navigate these few meters right ahead.

The combined effect of the two enables the robot to not only operate in accordance with the overall task, but also adapt to real-time environmental changes.

docs.title: 3.3 Coverage Planning
docs.text:
For robotic lawn mowers, another extremely important concept is Coverage Path Planning. While the goal of standard navigation is to move from point A to point B, the objective of coverage planning is to cover the entire working area as completely and efficiently as possible.

For example, the common Zigzag Pattern is essentially a type of coverage strategy. The algorithm needs to comprehensively take into account factors such as the shape of the working area, the width of the robot, the path spacing, the boundaries, and the turning space to generate the operation route.

Therefore, the question "why didn't the mowing robot strictly follow the sequence 1→2→3 to mow the lawn" does not necessarily indicate a path error. The system may readjust the execution order based on turning radius, remaining unmown area, path efficiency or real-time environment, and as long as the final goal of Coverage is met, such adjustment may still be a normal planning behavior.

docs.title: 3.4 Obstacle Detection \& Obstacle Avoidance
docs.text:
Obstacle Detection and Obstacle Avoidance are two related yet distinct concepts. Obstacle Detection addresses the question of "whether there is an object ahead and where it is", while Obstacle Avoidance deals with "what the robot should do after detecting such an object".

Cameras, LiDAR, ultrasonic sensors, ToF sensors, bumpers and other devices can all provide obstacle information. After the system obtains the position and distance of obstacles, it needs to make decisions by combining the robot's speed, direction, available space and original path.

Therefore:

Sensor → Obstacle Detection → Environment Understanding → Avoidance Decision → Motion Adjustment

Instead of performing the same action whenever any object is detected, the robot may choose to decelerate, stop, detour or re-plan its path depending on the specific situation.

docs.title: 3.5 Static \& Dynamic Obstacles
docs.text:
Obstacles can also be categorized into Static Obstacles and Dynamic Obstacles. The positions of trees, walls and fixed flower beds generally remain unchanged for a long time, so they can be regarded as part of the map; while people, pets or temporarily placed items may move at any time, thus their processing mainly relies on real-time environment perception.

This is also why robots typically require both Map + Real-Time Perception: the map tells the robot "what is usually here", while real-time perception tells it "what is actually here right now".

When the robot detects a temporary obstacle, the Local Planner can temporarily modify the current path; after the obstacle disappears, the robot can resume the original task without permanently modifying the entire base map.

docs.title: 4.1 Basic Principles of Docking
docs.text:
The goal of Docking (recharging docking) is to enable the robot to autonomously return to the charging pile and complete the final precise docking when it finishes work or needs to be charged. Different from ordinary Navigation, returning to the pile not only requires the robot to "arrive near the charging pile", but also requires the robot to enter the charging pile with sufficiently accurate position and orientation. Therefore, the entire process of returning to the pile can be divided into two main stages: Recahrging (recharging) and Docking (docking to the pile).

The overall logic can be simply expressed as follows:

Localization \& Navigation → Recharging → Within 5 m of Charging Station → Infrared Guidance → Fine Alignment → Docking

Different information is adopted in the two stages to accomplish tasks with different precisions: the positioning and navigation system is first responsible for bringing the robot to the vicinity of the charging pile, and then the infrared guidance takes charge of the precise docking in the final stage.

docs.title: 4.2 Recharging
docs.text:
When a robot needs to be charged, it first enters the Recharging process. The system uses the current Localization information, Map and Charging Station Position to plan the route back to the charging pile.

Essentially, this phase still falls under Navigation:

Robot Position + Charging Station Position → Path Planning → Navigation → Approach Charging Station

At this point, the system mainly addresses the following questions:"Where am I? ", "Where is the charging pile? ", and "How should I get back? "

The robot does not need to directly detect the charging contacts throughout the entire return process; instead, it first relies on Localization and Navigation to return to the vicinity of the Charging Station.

In the current product logic, when the robot enters a range approximately 5 m from the Charging Station, it can further enter the close-range Docking Guidance phase via Infrared Guidance.

Therefore, if the robot is completely unable to return to the vicinity of the Charging Station, priority should be given to Localization, Map, Charging Station Position and Navigation, rather than initially diagnosing it as an Infrared Guidance or Charging Hardware issue.

docs.title: 4.3 Docking
docs.text:
After the robot has returned to the vicinity of the Charging Station, the system needs to further complete Docking.

The problems addressed in this phase have shifted away from:"Where is the Charging Station located? "

Transformed into:"At what position and orientation should I enter the Charging Station? "

When the robot enters a range of approximately 5 m, it can further identify the direction of the Infrared Guidance to further recognize the direction of the Charging Station, and adjust its own movement so that the robot can correctly enter the charging pile.

It can be simply understood as: Localization \& Navigation → Bring Robot Near the Station

随后：Infrared Guidance → Approach \& Alignment → Docking

Therefore, Localization / Navigation mainly addresses the return problem in a relatively large range, while Infrared Guidance mainly solves the short-range guidance issue after approaching the Charging Station.

docs.title: 4.4 Charging
docs.text:
After Docking is completed, the robot still needs to establish a valid Charging Connection before it can truly enter the Charging state.

Therefore: Docked ≠ Charging

The fact that the robot has physically entered the Charging Station does not necessarily mean that charging has been successfully completed.

The normal process can be simply understood as follows:

Docking → Charging Contact Established → Charging Detected → Charging Starts

This phase involves the physical contact and electrical connection between the robot and the Charging Station. The robot can only enter the normal Charging State after the charging contacts are properly connected and the system detects valid charging conditions.

Therefore, if the robot can return normally and complete the docking to the charging pile, but ultimately fails to start charging, then Localization, Navigation, and Infrared Guidance have most likely completed their respective tasks. At this point, the scope of the problem should be further shifted to:

Charging Contact / Charging Station / Power Supply / Charging Detection / Charging Circuit

and other charging-related processes.

docs.title: 4.5 Obstacle Avoidance Logic for Docking Area
docs.text:
After the robot approaches the charging pile, Obstacle Avoidance is disabled by default. This is a key difference between the charging docking process and standard Navigation.

During normal operation, the robot needs to identify obstacles via its perception system and then stop or detour accordingly. However, the actual installation environment around the charging pile may be rather special; for example, users may add shelter structures similar to "dog houses" or other protective facilities outside the charging pile. If the robot still operates following the obstacle avoidance logic for ordinary working areas when near the charging pile, these structures may be recognized as obstacles, which will consequently prevent the robot from entering or leaving the charging pile properly.

Therefore, disabling the conventional obstacle avoidance function near the charging pile is to ensure that the robot can complete the actions of leaving and returning to the charging pile in accordance with the established Docking Logic, without having the obstacle avoidance triggered repeatedly by the fixed structures around the charging pile.

This also means that the Docking Area follows different motion and safety logics from regular work areas. When installing the charging pile, it is still necessary to ensure that there is space suitable for the robot to enter and exit near the charging pile in accordance with the product requirements.

docs.title: Algorithm System Summary - Relationships Between the Four Modules
docs.text:
Localization, Mapping \& SLAM, Navigation \& Obstacle Avoidance, and Docking are not four mutually independent functions; instead, they share information on localization, maps and environmental perception to jointly form the closed loop of autonomous operation for robots.

Localization serves as the foundation of the entire system, which is responsible for continuously determining the robot's position and motion status. Depending on the specific product, the robot can integrate various types of information including RTK / NetRTK, Vision, LiDAR, IMU, and Wheel Odometry to perform localization. As products iterate, the localization method has gradually evolved from being dominated by a single RTK to multi-sensor fusion, enabling the robot to utilize different localization information according to varying environmental conditions to maintain continuous and stable position estimation.

Mapping \& SLAM further builds the robot's spatial understanding of the surrounding environment based on localization. The robot observes the environment using perceptual information such as Vision and LiDAR, and constructs or updates a map in combination with its own position; meanwhile, visual or geometric features in the environment can in turn assist the robot in localization and Re-localization. Therefore, Localization and SLAM do not have a completely unidirectional relationship, but rather provide mutual information and corrections for each other.

After obtaining Robot Pose + Map + Real-Time Perception, Navigation \& Obstacle Avoidance determines how the robot will move next. Navigation performs path and coverage planning based on the current position, target position and map, while Obstacle Avoidance uses real-time perception information to handle temporarily emerging obstacles.With the development of product algorithms, the planning and control method can also evolve from Static Planning that mainly relies on fixed maps, to Dynamic Planning that integrates real-time positioning and environment perception information, so as to adjust the internal dynamic map and local boundaries during operation, and improve the coverage rate and operation continuity in complex environments.

When the robot completes its task or needs to be charged, the system initiates the recharging process. First, via Recharging, the system continues to leverage Localization, Map and Navigation to guide the robot from its current position back to the vicinity of the Charging Station.When the robot enters the area approximately 5 meters from the Charging Station, the system further proceeds to the Docking phase, and completes short-range orientation judgment, position adjustment and final docking via Infrared Guidance. Near the Charging Station, the robot adopts dedicated Docking Logic and disables conventional obstacle avoidance by default, so as to prevent the Charging Station and its surrounding fixed structures from blocking the robot's normal undocking or docking process.

After successful docking, the robot further needs to establish a valid charging connection and enter the Charging status. Therefore, docking and charging are two distinct concepts: docking addresses whether the robot can correctly access the charging station, while charging addresses whether the robot can establish a valid physical and electrical connection and start charging after being positioned on the charging station.

Therefore, from the perspective of the information flow of the entire autonomous robot operation, the relationship among the four main algorithm modules can be summarized as follows:

Sensors → Localization / SLAM → Robot Pose + Map → Navigation \& Obstacle Avoidance → Motion → Sensor Feedback

When the robot needs to return for charging, it will further enter:

Localization \& Navigation → Recharging → Near Charging Station (\~5 m) → Infrared Guidance → Docking → Charging Connection → Charging

It should be noted that this is not a strictly unidirectional process, but a closed loop of continuous feedback and correction. For example, environment perception can help SLAM and Localization update the position, the new localization result will affect Navigation, and the motion generated by Navigation will in turn bring new Sensor Data, thereby updating the localization and map again. During the recharging process, the position and status of the robot will also change continuously, which will affect the subsequent Recharging and Docking behaviors.

Understanding such upstream and downstream dependencies is particularly important, because the anomalies ultimately exhibited by a robot do not necessarily stem from the malfunctioning function itself. For instance, path deviation may arise from positioning errors, abnormal detours may originate from environment perception or planning and control logic, while issues related to automatic charging can be further divided into three stages:

Failure to return to the vicinity of the Charging Station → Recharging / Localization / Navigation

Returned to the vicinity but unable to dock → Docking / Infrared Guidance

Successfully connected to the charging pile but unable to start charging → Charging Connection / Charging System

Therefore, when troubleshooting issues, you can follow the steps below:

Sensor Input → Localization / Map → Planning → Recharging → Docking → Charging

Gradually determine which functional phase the abnormality occurs in, so as to avoid classifying all problems of "failure to recharge normally" as Docking Failure.

docs.title: Embedded System Principle Knowledge
docs.text:
An embedded system is a core control and information processing platform that connects robot algorithms, sensors, actuators, and external networks. During the operation of a robot, sensors continuously collect information about the robot's own status and the surrounding environment; SoCs and MCUs calculate and process this information, convert the decisions generated by algorithms into low-level control instructions, which are finally executed by actuators.Meanwhile, robots also need to exchange information with Apps, Cloud, RTK systems and other external devices via wireless connection methods such as 4G, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and LoRa.

From the perspective of the complete machine, a basic information chain of Sensor → SoC / MCU → Control → Actuator is formed inside the robot. After the Actuator performs an action, the robot's status and the surrounding environment change, and the Sensor acquires new information again and feeds it back to the system, thus forming a complete closed loop of Sensing → Processing → Decision → Control → Execution → Feedback.

Meanwhile, the robot also connects to external systems via the App ↔ Cloud ↔ Robot architecture. The Cloud further supports IoT functions including Binding, OTA Upgrade, Map Backup, and Data Center. Therefore, the embedded system serves not only as a platform for algorithm operation but also as the core system connecting Sensors, Algorithms, Hardware, Communications, and the Cloud.

This module is mainly divided into six chapters: Embedded System Architecture, SoC \& MCU, Sensor \& Actuator Interface, Internal Communication, Wireless Communication \& Connectivity, as well as IoT, Cloud \& App.

docs.title: Embedded System Architecture  Complete Machine Embedded Architecture
1.1 Basic Composition of Embedded Systems
docs.text:
A robot does not have a single processor that directly performs all its functions; instead, it is composed of multiple functional modules with distinct roles. Based on the functions of each module in the system, the entire embedded system can be roughly categorized into Sensing, Computing, Control, Execution, and Connectivity components.

Sensors serve as the information input terminals of the system, responsible for acquiring the robot's own status and surrounding environmental information, such as Bumper, Emergency Stop, LiDAR, Vision, Ultrasonic and other sensors or system statuses. SoCs and MCUs constitute the main Computing \& Control Platform of the robot, which processes the input information and generates corresponding algorithmic or control results.Actuator serves as the execution end of the system, such as Wheel Motor, Cutter Motor and Lift Motor, which is responsible for converting electronic control instructions into actual actions.

Therefore, the most fundamental information relationship inside a robot can be expressed as follows:

Sensor → SoC / MCU → Actuator

However, robots do not operate in a unidirectional manner based on fixed instructions. After the Actuator performs an action, the robot's own state and the external environment change, and the Sensor will reacquire new information and feed it back to the control system. Therefore, a continuous feedback closed loop is formed during the actual operation:

Sensor → Processing → Decision → Control → Actuator → Feedback

docs.title: 1.2 Data Flow \& Control Flow
docs.text:
When understanding robotic embedded systems, a further distinction can be made between Data Flow and Control Flow.

Data Flow mainly describes how information enters the system from sensors. For example, a Camera generates Image Data, LiDAR produces environmental distance and geometric information, an IMU provides motion and posture data, while sensors such as Bumper and Emergency Stop deliver corresponding Trigger / Status Information. These data will be sent to the SoC or MCU according to functional and real-time requirements.

Control Flow describes how control information is transmitted to the actuators after the system makes a decision. For example, after the Navigation Algorithm determines that the robot needs to move forward, the system needs to convert this High-Level Decision into low-level motion control commands, and then drive the Motor through the control system.

Therefore, the complete process can be understood as follows:

Sensor Data → Processing → Algorithm / Logic → Control Command → Actuator → Feedback

This is also why a robot's function is usually not accomplished by a single sensor, algorithm or hardware alone, but relies on continuous data exchange between multiple modules.

docs.title: 1.3 Relationship between Embedded System and Algorithm / Hardware
docs.text:
The three modules, namely Algorithm, Embedded System and Hardware, are interrelated yet play distinct roles.

Algorithm mainly addresses what a robot should do, such as determining its current location, selecting the appropriate navigation path, and judging whether obstacle avoidance is required;Embedded System is responsible for issues including where Sensor Data is processed, where the algorithm runs, how information is exchanged between different modules, and how Algorithm Decision is converted into control commands;Hardware provides the actual capabilities of perception, power supply, driving and execution.

Therefore, the relationship among the three can be simply understood as follows:

Sensor / Hardware → Embedded System → Algorithm → Embedded System → Hardware / Actuator

Embedded System lies between Algorithm and Hardware, serving as the connection hub for the Data Flow and Control Flow of the entire machine.

docs.title: SoC \& MCU Computing and Control Platform
2.1 Basic Concepts of SoC and MCU
docs.text:
SoC (System on Chip) and MCU (Microcontroller Unit) are two crucial computing and Control Units inside a robot. Both are capable of running software and processing data, but they typically undertake different tasks.

SoCs typically feature robust computing and data processing capabilities, making them better suited for running algorithms with heavy computational loads such as Vision, Localization, SLAM, Navigation, and AI Recognition. As such, an SoC can be understood as the High-Level Computing Platform of a robot.

MCUs are better suited for handling low-level control tasks that demand high real-time performance and have relatively clear objectives, such as Sensor status reading, Motor Control, Actuator Control, and Safety Signal Monitoring. Therefore, an MCU can be regarded as the Real-Time Control Platform of a robot.

The basic division of responsibilities between the two can be summarized as follows:

SoC → Perception / Localization / Planning / High-Level Computing

MCU → Sensor Monitoring / Real-Time Control / Actuator Control

docs.title: 2.2 Why both SoC and MCU are required
docs.text:
A high-performance SoC does not mean that robots no longer need MCUs, as these two types of processors address different types of problems.

Cameras and LiDARs generate a large amount of environmental data, which requires relatively complex computation before being applied to vision, localization and environment understanding, making them more suitable to be processed by SoCs. The algorithm running on the SoC can determine the next movement of the robot based on environmental, map and localization information.

However, "the robot should move forward" remains merely a High-Level Decision. When actually executing this action, the system also needs to continuously control the speeds of the left and right wheels, read Motor Feedback, monitor the Sensor State, and make constant adjustments based on the actual execution status. Such real-time control tasks are better suited for MCUs.

Therefore, a typical information link can be understood as follows:

Vision / LiDAR / Localization Data → SoC → Motion Decision → MCU → Actuator

At the same time, the underlying state will feed back upward:

Sensor / Actuator Feedback → MCU → SoC → Algorithm

SoC and MCU connect High-Level Algorithm with Low-Level Control through continuous data exchange.

docs.title: 2.3 Relationship between Different Sensors and SoC/MCU
docs.text:
Not all sensor data must first enter the SoC. Depending on the data volume, processing method and real-time requirements, different sensors can be processed by either the SoC or the MCU.

Sensors such as Camera and LiDAR generate a large amount of data, and usually need to participate in Vision, Localization, SLAM and Environment Perception, so they are mainly related to the high-level algorithms running on the SoC.

Information provided by sensors such as Bumper and Emergency Stop is relatively simple, yet requires high response speed, so it can be processed quickly by the MCU or the corresponding real-time control system.

It can be simply understood as:

Complex Environment Data → SoC

Real-Time Status / Control Signal → MCU

The specific data path varies depending on the hardware architecture and functional design of different products.

docs.title: 2.4 Product Evolution of SoC + MCU
docs.text:
As the functions of robots continue to expand, the requirements for the Computing Platform of products are also rising. When the functions and Sensors of early products were relatively simple, MCUs could undertake more control tasks; with the addition of functions such as Vision, LiDAR, SLAM and Multi-Sensor Localization, the data volume and algorithm complexity have increased significantly, so it is necessary to introduce SoCs with stronger performance.

The product computing platform can gradually evolve from an MCU-centric setup to SoC + MCU Architecture, and further upgrade the computing power of the SoC in line with algorithm requirements, for instance, advancing from the X3 platform to the X5 platform.

However, in this process, MCUs have not been replaced by SoCs. The performance improvement of SoCs mainly supports more complex Perception and Algorithm Processing, while MCUs continue to be responsible for low-level real-time control and hardware management. Therefore, the development of product computing platforms essentially evolves from relatively simple control systems to a collaborative architecture of High-Level Computing + Real-Time Control.

docs.title: Sensor \& Actuator Interface: Perception Input and Actuation Output
3.1 The Role of Sensors in Embedded Systems
docs.text:
Sensor serves as the interface through which robots obtain information about their own status and the external environment. The Sensor itself is responsible for detecting and collecting information, while the SoC, MCU and Algorithm further process this data to determine how the robot should respond.

Based on the actual functions of the robot, the relevant inputs can be simply understood as different types.

Contact Sensor (Contact-type Sensor) is triggered by physical contact or changes in mechanical status, such as Bumper, Emergency Stop, and some types of Lift Detection. This type of Sensor usually provides relatively clear status information and is frequently involved in basic safety and status judgment.

Non-contact Sensors do not require direct physical contact with the target, typical examples include vision sensors, LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors. They are primarily responsible for collecting information about the surrounding environment, and further support functions such as perception, localization and obstacle detection.

The system may also contain Logic / Derived State formed based on one or more Sensor Signals. For example, the system can synthesize data from the Wheel, IMU and the robot's motion state to determine whether a Slip has occurred. Such states do not necessarily correspond to an independent physical Sensor, but may be results calculated by the system from multiple inputs.

docs.title: 3.2 How Sensor Data Enters the System
docs.text:
Different sensors generate data types and volumes that vary significantly. For example, a bumper may only need to report a Triggered / Not Triggered status, while a camera continuously generates large volumes of image data, and LiDAR continuously produces environmental distance and geometric information.

Therefore, the processing paths for different Sensors may also vary:

Simple State Sensor → MCU / Controller

Vision / LiDAR → SoC → Perception Algorithm

These pieces of information from different sources are ultimately further utilized by the Algorithm and Control System.

Therefore, a normal Sensor does not necessarily mean that the final function is normal. A complete function usually needs to go through the following processes:

Sensor → Data Transfer → Processing → Decision → Control

Any abnormality in any of these links may eventually manifest as a functional failure of the robot.

docs.title: 3.3 Actuator
docs.text:
Actuator is responsible for converting electronic control instructions into actual physical actions. Typical actuators in robots include wheel motors, cutter motors, lift motors, and other motion execution mechanisms.

Actuators are generally not directly controlled by high-level Algorithms, but are implemented through low-level control systems and Drivers. For example:

Navigation Decision → Motion Command → MCU / Controller → Motor Driver → Wheel Motor

After the Motor performs an action, its Speed, Current, Position or other status can be fed back to the control system again, thus forming Closed-Loop Control:

Command → Actuator → Feedback → Controller → Adjustment

Therefore, from a systematic perspective, it can be simply understood as follows:

Sensor = What is happening?

SoC / MCU = What should the system do?

Actuator = Execute the action.

docs.title: 4.1 Why Internal Communication Is Needed
docs.text:
Inside a robot, there are components including SoC, MCU, Sensor, Driver, Battery/BMS, and other electronic modules. These modules do not operate independently of one another; instead, they require continuous exchange of data and control information.

For example, after the SoC calculates the new Motion Decision, it needs to transmit the relevant information to the MCU; after the MCU completes the control operation, it needs to return the Hardware Status, Sensor State and Error Information to the SoC.

Therefore, there is a large amount of two-way information exchange inside the robot:

SoC ↔ MCU

Controller ↔ Sensor

Controller ↔ Driver / Actuator

Internal Communication can be understood as the "information channel" between different electronic modules of a robot.

docs.title: 4.2 Command、Status \& Feedback
docs.text:
The information exchanged in internal communication can be simply divided into Command, Status and Feedback.

A Command indicates what the control system expects another module to execute, such as Target Speed, Start/Stop, or other action requirements; a Status represents the current state of a module, such as Ready, Running, Stopped, or Error; while Feedback is used to inform the control system of the actual execution result, such as Actual Speed, Position, Current, or Sensor State.

Therefore, a typical control process can be expressed as follows:

Command → Module → Execution → Feedback → Controller

Robots rely on this continuous exchange of information to determine whether an instruction has actually been executed, and decide whether further adjustments are necessary based on the feedback.

docs.title: 4.3 Communication Exception
docs.text:
When internal modules fail to exchange information properly, the corresponding function may not work normally even if the relevant Hardware itself is not damaged.

For example, the SoC may have generated a correct Motion Decision, but if the control information fails to be properly transmitted to the MCU or the execution module, the robot may still exhibit "no action"; conversely, if the hardware has executed the action normally but the status cannot be fed back to the upper-level system, the upper-level system may also judge it as abnormal.

Therefore, for a functional anomaly, it is necessary to distinguish between:

Device / Hardware → Communication → Controller / Software

That is to say:

Hardware Exception ≠ Communication Exception

Specific products may internally adopt different communication interfaces and protocols. For Distis/Dealers, the priority is not to master the underlying communication timing, but to understand that stable data communication between modules is required for them to jointly complete a function.

docs.title: Wireless Communication \& Connectivity
docs.text:
Robots not only need to exchange data between their internal modules, but also need to establish connections with external devices such as Phone, Internet, Cloud, RTK Service or other external devices. Different Wireless Technologies are responsible for different types of information transmission.

First, it is necessary to distinguish:

Data Communication → Bluetooth / Wi-Fi / 4G / LoRa

Positioning Signal → GNSS

They can exist in a robot at the same time, but perform different functions.

docs.title: 5.1 Bluetooth
docs.text:
Bluetooth is mainly used for Short-Range Local Communication between a robot and nearby devices, such as establishing a local connection between a Smartphone and a Robot.

Phone ↔ Bluetooth ↔ Robot

Bluetooth is therefore more suitable for Nearby Connection, Configuration and Local Operation than for long-distance Cloud Connection.

docs.title: 5.2 Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Wi-Fi is primarily used for robots to connect to local networks, and further access the Internet and Cloud via a Router.

Robot → Wi-Fi → Router → Internet → Cloud

Special distinction is required:

Wi-Fi Connected ≠ Internet Connected ≠ Cloud Connected

Even if a robot is already connected to a Router, the relevant Cloud Function may still be unavailable if the Router does not have Internet access.

docs.title: 5.3 4G
docs.text:
4G/cellular networks provide wide-area internet connectivity for robots.

Robot → 4G Network → Internet → Cloud

Therefore, the robot does not need to be within the coverage of home Wi-Fi all the time to access the Remote / Cloud Service.

In the NetRTK scenario, 4G can also undertake the network transmission of Correction Data, however:

4G = Data Connection ≠ Positioning

High-precision positioning still relies on GNSS Signal and effective RTK Correction Data.

docs.title: 5.4 LoRa
docs.text:
LoRa is a wireless technology designed for Long-Range + Low-Data-Rate Communication, which is suitable for transmitting small amounts of Status, Command or other Small Data Packet between devices.

Device A ↔ LoRa ↔ Device B

Therefore, its positioning is not completely the same as that of Wi-Fi / 4G:

Wi-Fi / 4G → Internet / Cloud Connection

LoRa → Long-Range Device-to-Device Communication

The specific function that LoRa undertakes in robots needs to be determined according to the specific product architecture.

docs.title: 5.5 GNSS
docs.text:
GNSS differs from the preceding technologies. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, 4G and LoRa are primarily responsible for Data Communication, while the core function of GNSS is Satellite Positioning.

GNSS Satellites → GNSS Signal → Robot Receiver → Position

GPS, Galileo, BeiDou, GLONASS and other systems all fall under the category of GNSS.

GNSS, RTK and Communication Link need to be clearly distinguished:

GNSS → Satellite Positioning

RTK / NetRTK → Correction → Higher Positioning Accuracy

4G / Wi-Fi / LoRa → Data Transmission（depending on product architecture）

For example, NetRTK can utilize both GNSS and network communication simultaneously:

Satellite → GNSS Signal → Robot RTK Service → Internet → Robot

Both types of information ultimately participate in high-precision positioning together.

docs.title: 6.1 Basic Concepts of IoT
docs.text:
IoT (Internet of Things) enables robots to exchange information with clouds, apps and backend services via the network.

In a robotic system, the basic architecture can be understood as: App ↔ Cloud ↔ Robot

Wherein:

Robot → Executes tasks and generates Device Data ** Cloud → Connects Robot, User Account and Cloud Services ** App → Provides entry for user operation and device management

Therefore, IoT is not an independent Hardware Module inside a robot, but a system consisting of:

Robot + Connectivity + Internet + Cloud + App

together form a system.

docs.title: 6.2 Local Function \& Cloud Function
docs.text:
Some functions of the robot can be implemented via Local Connection, while Remote Service usually requires the Internet and Cloud.

It can be simply understood as:

Local：Phone ↔ Robot

Cloud：App ↔ Cloud ↔ Robot

Therefore：Robot Connected ≠ Internet Available ≠ Cloud Service Available

When troubleshooting issues, it is necessary to distinguish whether the fault occurs in Robot, Connectivity, Internet or Cloud Service.

docs.title: 6.3 Binding
docs.text:
Binding is used to establish: User Account ↔ Robot Identity

the device affiliation relationship between them, which is usually managed by Cloud.

Therefore, it can be understood as follows:

User Account → Cloud ← Robot Identity ↓ Binding Relationship

Binding essentially belongs to Device Management Logic, rather than Bluetooth/Wi-Fi itself.

Therefore, when a device cannot be added by a new Account, it does not necessarily mean that there is a problem with the Robot Hardware or Wireless Communication, and the current Binding State should also be taken into consideration.

docs.title: 6.4 OTA Upgrade
docs.text:
OTA (Over-the-Air) Upgrade refers to the mechanism of delivering firmware updates to robots via the internet.

The basic process is as follows:

Firmware Package → Cloud → Robot → Firmware Update

Robots may incorporate SoCs, MCUs and other electronic modules inside, so the firmware system may also consist of multiple components.

Therefore, the normal operation of the system not only relies on Hardware, but also on the compatibility between different Software / Firmware Components:

Hardware + Firmware + Communication → Stable System Operation

Therefore, a Firmware-related Exception does not necessarily indicate Hardware Damage.

docs.title: 6.5 Map Backup
docs.text:
Mapping/SLAM is responsible for generating and updating maps, while the Cloud Service can take charge of the Backup/Synchronization of the generated Map Data.

A clear distinction must be made between the two:

Mapping / SLAM → Create / Update Map

Cloud Service → Backup / Synchronize Map

The basic data link can be understood as: Robot Map → Cloud → Backup / Synchronization

docs.title: 6.6 Data Center
docs.text:
During operation, the robot generates Status, Operation, Error, and Diagnostic Data and other types of information. Depending on the specific product design, some of these data may be uploaded to the Cloud / Data Center via the network for device status monitoring, issue analysis, and after-sales support.

The basic link is as follows: Robot Data → Connectivity → Cloud / Data Center

Essentially, the data displayed in the backend originates from the internal system of the Robot, and is then uploaded via the Network and Cloud Chain.

Therefore：No Data in Cloud ≠ No Data Generated by Robot

If there is no data in the backend, it is necessary to further determine where the problem occurs:

Robot → Connectivity → Internet → Cloud / Data Center which link in the chain.

docs.title: Embedded System — Relationships Between Modules
docs.text:
The core function of a robot embedded system is to connect Sensor, Algorithm, Control, Actuator, Communication and Cloud, enabling different modules to jointly realize the autonomous operation of the robot.

Inside the robot, the Sensor first acquires its own status and environmental information: Sensor → SoC / MCU

SoC is primarily responsible for high-level computing tasks such as Perception, Localization, SLAM and Navigation, while the MCU is mainly in charge of Sensor Monitoring, Real-Time Control and Actuator Control.The Decision generated by the Algorithm is further transmitted to the actuator through the control system: SoC → MCU / Controller → Actuator

The execution result is then fed back again: Actuator / Sensor Feedback → MCU / SoC

Therefore, the internal structure of a robot is formed as follows: Sensor → Processing → Decision → Control → Actuator → Feedback

Different electronic modules continuously exchange data with each other via Internal Communication:

Command ↔ Status ↔ Feedback ↔ Error Information

Outside the robot, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, 4G and LoRa provide data communication capabilities for different application scenarios, while GNSS offers Satellite Positioning Information: Robot ↔ Wireless Connectivity ↔ External Device / Internet

At the IoT level, the following architecture is further formed: App ↔ Cloud ↔ Robot

Cloud supports functions including Binding, OTA Upgrade, Map Backup, and Data Center.

Therefore, from the perspective of the complete machine, the complete information relationship of the Embedded System can be summarized as follows:

Environment / Sensor / GNSS → SoC \& MCU → Algorithm \& Control → Actuator → Robot State → Sensor Feedback

同时：Robot ↔ Bluetooth / Wi-Fi / 4G / LoRa ↔ App / Cloud / External Service

Understanding the significance of this system relationship lies in the fact that: an anomaly ultimately exhibited by a robot does not necessarily mean that the Hardware where the abnormal performance occurs is itself damaged. For a function to be executed from Sensor Input to the final implementation, it may sequentially go through Sensor, SoC/MCU, Internal Communication, Algorithm, Control and Actuator;A Cloud Function may further involve Wireless Connection, Internet, Cloud and Account.

Therefore, when analyzing issues related to Embedded Systems, you can follow the sequence of Input → Processing → Communication → Control → Execution → Feedback to identify which stage the problem occurs in, so as to provide a systematic basis for subsequent troubleshooting.

docs.text:
Figure 1. LUBA 3 Board Link Diagram.

This chapter explains how the robot's power supply, charging system, motor drives, feedback signals and safety hardware work together. The connection diagram identifies physical components and wiring; the sections below explain their functional relationships. Circuit details, test points and limits must be checked against the service documentation for the relevant model.

docs.title: 1.1 How the Systems Work Together
docs.text:
A motor needs more than a start command. It needs a suitable power supply, a functioning driver, valid operating permission and a mechanical assembly that can move. The controller also needs reliable feedback to confirm that the requested action has occurred.

System Role in Operation Power and battery Supply the electronics and motor drives through the relevant power paths. Charging Transfer power from the charging station into the battery under controlled conditions. Control Set the requested action and coordinate execution. Motor drive and feedback Apply controlled power to the motor and report its operating state. Safety hardware Provide safety inputs and, depending on the design, inhibit or interrupt hazardous outputs.

These functions may share a board or be distributed across several boards. A board name does not define the full boundary of a system: a motor drive includes its power connection, control interface, output stage, motor wiring and feedback path.

docs.title: 1.2 What a Hardware Symptom Tells Us
docs.text:
A symptom identifies the function that failed, rather than the component that caused it. A wheel that does not turn may have a supply problem, an inhibited driver, a faulty connection, unreliable feedback or a mechanical obstruction.

When several functions fail together, look for a shared supply, controller or connection. When one function fails, inspect its local path first. These observations help prioritize checks; they do not establish the root cause on their own.

docs.title: 2.1 Battery Output and Power Distribution
docs.text:
The battery supplies both the robot electronics and the motor drives. Power distribution and voltage conversion provide the conditions required by each load, while switches and protection circuits determine whether a path is enabled.

A successful startup confirms that the electronics receive enough power to start. It does not confirm that every supply branch is healthy or that the battery can support a motor load. A weak battery or a high-resistance connector may appear normal at rest but cause a voltage drop when a motor starts, resulting in reduced output, module resets or shutdown.

docs.title: 2.2 Battery Management and Protection
docs.text:
The battery management system (BMS) monitors and protects the battery according to its design, using information such as cell voltage, current and temperature. It can restrict charging or discharging when operating conditions exceed permitted limits.

An interrupted power supply can therefore be caused by battery protection rather than a damaged driveboard. Check battery condition, output under load, connectors and protection status together. The displayed charge level alone is insufficient to establish battery health or available output capability.

docs.title: 3.1 Docking and Charging Are Different Processes
docs.text:
Docking places the robot at the charging station. Charging requires a continuous electrical path from the adapter, through the station and mating contacts, to the robot's charging circuit and battery.

The charging circuit controls the electrical conditions applied to the battery. Battery state and protection conditions can prevent charging even when external power is available. Successful docking therefore does not prove that contact is established or that charging has started.

docs.title: 3.2 Contact Quality and Installation
docs.text:
Charging depends on stable contact alignment and pressure. Dirt, oxidation, worn contacts, uneven ground or a tilted station can cause intermittent contact or increased resistance. Increased resistance can produce voltage drop and heating when charging current flows, even if contact appears present.

For a robot that docks but does not charge, distinguish three questions: does the station provide the required output, does that output reach the robot reliably, and does the battery accept charging? Check the adapter and station, contact condition and alignment, internal wiring and charging circuit, then battery state and protection reasons. Use the model-specific connection diagram to locate each part of this path.
