docs.title: 4.1 Controller Driver and Motor
docs.text:
The controller specifies the requested direction, speed or position. The driver switches power to the motor to produce the required torque and movement. Feedback allows the controller to compare the actual state with the target and adjust output or stop operation.

The control signal and motor power supply are separate requirements. A valid command cannot produce movement if the driver lacks power or is disabled. Conversely, a powered driver does not guarantee that it has received a valid command or reliable feedback.

docs.title: 4.2 Motor Functions and Mechanical Load
docs.text:
Motor Function Required Result Relevant Checks Wheel drive Produce the requested wheel movement. Drive output, motor feedback, wheel resistance and ground interaction. Cutting Maintain cutter rotation under the cutting load. Grass load, entanglement, obstruction, mechanical resistance and current. Height adjustment Move the mechanism to the requested height. Drive output, transmission movement and position or state feedback.

Higher mechanical load generally requires greater torque and current. Dense grass, entanglement, a blocked disc or a tight bearing can therefore trigger overcurrent or overload protection without the motor itself being damaged. If the fault persists under normal low-load conditions, investigate the drive stage, motor, wiring and current-sensing path as well as the mechanics.

docs.title: 4.3 Feedback and Hall Signals
docs.text:
Feedback provides evidence of motor rotation, speed or mechanism position. In designs that use motor Hall sensors, their signals can support rotor-position detection, commutation and speed measurement. The exact use depends on the drive design.

A motor may be mechanically capable of turning while its feedback is unreliable. A Hall fault can originate in the sensor, its supply, a connector, the feedback wiring or the receiving circuit. Persistent faults require hardware inspection because reliable operation cannot be assumed from visible movement alone.

Current feedback serves a different purpose: it helps regulate torque and detect excessive electrical or mechanical load. Interpret current together with movement and operating conditions. A command with little movement and high current suggests a different failure path from a command with no drive output.

docs.title: 5.1 Safety Inputs and Output Inhibition
docs.text:
Safety hardware converts a physical condition into an electrical state. An emergency-stop mechanism, safety key or lift-related sensor may use contacts or a sensor to provide that state. Depending on the design, it is evaluated by the controller, a dedicated safety circuit or both.

The resulting action may inhibit the drive stage, request a controlled stop or interrupt a relevant power path. A stop command and an inhibited power stage are different mechanisms, although both can prevent movement. The required response can also differ between wheel and cutter drives.

docs.title: 5.2 Safety Key and Drive Permission
docs.text:
The safety key provides an operating interlock. Removing it can prevent hazardous outputs while leaving the main electronics powered. The robot may therefore remain available for status checks even though motor operation is prohibited.

Possible implementations include a controller-detected key input, a hardware signal that disables the driver, or switching devices that interrupt a relevant circuit. The connection diagram alone cannot establish which implementation is used. Inserting the key satisfies one condition; it does not override other safety or protection conditions.

If key removal makes the wheels easier to turn, the driver may have released active holding or electrical braking and entered a high-impedance, or coasting, state. This can be achieved by switching off the power-stage MOSFETs without physically disconnecting the motor wires. The reduced resistance does not, by itself, identify whether the change was commanded by software or enforced by hardware.

docs.title: 5.3 Emergency Stop and Safety Sensors
docs.text:
An emergency stop provides a direct physical input for stopping or preventing hazardous operation. Other safety-related inputs report conditions such as lifting or displacement of a monitored mechanism. Their response is defined by the product's safety design.

When operation is inhibited, compare the physical condition with the state reported by the system. A mismatch may indicate a faulty contact or sensor, incorrect alignment, a wiring problem or an input-circuit fault. A correctly detected unsafe condition is a valid reason for stopping, rather than evidence of hardware damage.

docs.title: 5.4 Hardware Protection
docs.text:
Overcurrent, abnormal voltage and excessive temperature can also restrict output to protect the battery, driver or motor. Determine what triggered protection before deciding which part to replace.

Removing the safety key is not proof that the entire robot is electrically isolated. Follow the model-specific shutdown and isolation procedure before servicing, and do not bypass safety inputs during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Applying the System View
docs.text: For any hardware fault, identify the requested action, the power path, the drive or charging output, the relevant feedback and the safety conditions. Verify the suspected link under controlled conditions, change one factor at a time and repeat the original operating scenario after repair. This connects the observed symptom to a tested cause instead of assuming that the component named in the error is defective.

docs.title: RTK
docs.text:
RTK（Real-Time Kinematic / Antenna Over Datalink）： This is a traditional physical local area connection mode. The lawn mower and the RTK base station (user-installed) primarily perform direct transmission and handshaking of positioning error correction data (RTCM) through dedicated local physical radio communication (e.g., LoRa). This mode does not require any internet traffic at all, but it is limited by the physical radio frequency distance between the base station and the lawn mower, and the signal can be easily blocked by physical obstacles such as thick walls.

LoRa（Antenna Over Datalink）is a local physical radio communication technology. In the robotic mower system, its core concept and features are as follows:

  • Core Function : Enables point-to-point direct connection between the RTK base station and the mower unit, specifically responsible for transmitting positioning error correction data packets (RTCM) and heartbeat signals.

  • Network-Free : Pure physical radio frequency transmission, completely independent of home WiFi and consuming no 4G mobile data.

  • Physical Limitations : Constrained by the physical distance between the base station and the mower; RF signals are easily attenuated or blocked by large physical obstacles such as thick walls and buildings. The effective maximum range of LoRa is between 150 and 200 meters, and occasional base station disconnections may occur due to excessive distance from the base station.

docs.title: NRTK/iNavi Service
docs.text: NRTK（Network RTK / Antenna Over Internet): This is an internet-based network connection mode. In this mode, the RTK base station (public base station) uploads error correction data to the cloud server via home WiFi, and the mower then downloads these positioning data from the cloud through its own 4G or WiFi. It completely breaks the distance and occlusion limitations of physical radio waves, but heavily relies on the bidirectional internet connection stability between the base station and the mower end (network fluctuations easily cause frequent disconnections).

docs.title: LiDAR
docs.text: LiDAR（Light Detection and Ranging Positioning）：An active 3D spatial perception technology. The module on the top of the body rotates 360° to emit laser beams, and calculates the Time of Flight (ToF) of laser reflection to accurately measure the distance to the surrounding environment and obstacles, thereby constructing a high-precision 3D "point cloud map" in real time in the machine's brain. It does not rely on satellite signals from the sky at all. In the Tri-Fusion navigation system, when the machine drives into "signal black holes" such as extremely dense woods and high-wall corridors where RTK satellite signals are lost, LiDAR can instantly take over navigation and continue to travel accurately relying on physical contours.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text: Vision Positioning（Stereo Camera）：The core lies in SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and VIO (Visual Inertial Odometry). It does not care about what specific objects are in the picture, but specifically tracks "feature points (such as ground texture, brick edges)" in consecutive image frames. By calculating the pixel displacement of these feature points and combining with the chassis IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) data, it accurately back-calculates the machine's movement distance, rotation angle and absolute coordinates. When the machine drives into "black hole areas" such as dense woods and deep eaves where RTK satellite signals are completely lost, visual positioning will instantly take over. As long as the ground has rich texture, the machine can continue to "blind walk" smoothly relying on feature point tracking, perfectly eliminating positioning dead zones.

docs.title: Comparison of four positioing methods
docs.text: Positioning Method Advantages Disadvantages RTK Network-independent : Local physical radio direct connection, no data consumption, extremely stable connection as long as there is no occlusion. Occlusion-sensitive : Base station needs to be installed by the user, and work efficiency may be affected in occluded areas nRTK/iNavi Distance and occlusion resistant : Data transmitted via cloud, breaking through limitations of physical structures and transmission distance. No need to install a private base station. Unstable WiFi/4G signals can also impact operational efficiency LiDAR Signal blackhole solution : Active light emission for ranging and point cloud generation, satellite-independent, seamlessly takes over navigation under trees and in corridors. It is prone to recognition errors in large, featureless environments Vision Secondary backup line : Captures environmental feature points to calculate displacement, enabling precise "blind navigation" without satellite signals. Its functionality may be restricted under pure white walls, textureless glass, or low-light nighttime conditions

docs.title: Pre-Installation Check
docs.text: Goal: Ensure you have all the parts, tools, and correct preparation before touching the lawn.

docs.title: Unboxing and Verification
docs.text:
• Packaging undamaged, seal intact.

  • Verify all items are present:

    • mower User manual / quick-start guide

    • 3D Vision Module (Luba Series).

    • Front Bumper (Luba2x).

    • RTK Reference Station and radio antenna.

    • Power supply and cables for RTK and charging stations.

    • Accessory kit.

    • Mounting hardware (stakes, screws, brackets, pole, etc.).

    • Robot.

    • Charging station.

docs.title: Preliminary Checks
docs.text:
• Inspect robots and charging contacts for transport damage.

  • Verify software/app readiness: customer phone has the Mammotion app installed, account ready.

  • Confirm internet/Wi-Fi password available (2.4 GHz network for RTK, 5GHz for Robot).

docs.title: Robot Assembly
docs.text:
• (Luba 2X) Attach front bumper securely; verify alignment and free movement.

  • (Luba Series) Mount vision module (camera) as per manual, ensure connector clicks firmly.

  • Check cable routing: no pinched or twisted cables.

docs.title: Charging Station
docs.text:
• Choose a flat, stable, dry surface.

  • Ensure the station faces open lawn, not walls or fences.

  • Avoid walls, trees, fences, or metal objects nearby.

  • Minimum 1.5 m clearance in front, 0.5 m on each side.

  • Connect power supply, check LED indicator.

  • Fix the charging station to the ground using provided bolts.

  • Connect power supply and ensure LED indicator is on.

  • Place the robot on station and verify proper alignment of charging contacts.

docs.title: RTK Base Station Setup (if applicable)
docs.text:
• Place base station in fully open sky area, ideally with 360° horizon.

  • Mount securely using pole or wall bracket; confirm it’s level and stable.

  • Connect antenna and power; wait for RTK fixed signal.

  • Verify robot connection in app and RTK correction signal strength.

docs.title: Robot Connection
docs.text:
• When the robot powers on, connect it to the Mammotion App:

    • Bluetooth

    • Wi-Fi

    • Firmware update if required.

docs.title: Mapping & Calibration
docs.text:
• Document installation (If allowed): take photos of charging station and RTK placement.

  • Start “Mapping Mode” in app.

  • Drive robot manually or let it auto-map boundary.

  • Define zones and no-go areas (pools, trees, flowerbeds).

  • Save maps, check boundaries visually on app maps.

  • Test return-to-dock and start of mowing route.

docs.title: Functional Tests
docs.text:
• Start the first mowing session in a small test zone.

  • Observe mowing patterns, obstacle avoidance, and turning behavior.

  • Check obstacle sensors (camera, ultrasonic, bumper) react correctly.

  • Confirm robot resumes and docks for charging when done.

docs.title: Customer Handover
docs.text:
• Demonstrate app features (start/stop, scheduling, no-go zones).

  • Explain emergency stop and manual towing procedure.

  • Instruct on cleaning and maintenance (deck, blades, charging contacts).

  • Advise on firmware updates and seasonal storage.
